title: Enforcement priorities, resources, and disclosure
summary: Enforcement discretion includes decisions about which violations to investigate, pursue, settle, or leave unaddressed with limited resources.
notes:
The introductory materials contrast judicial protection from unlawful coercion with requests that courts stimulate enforcement for regulatory beneficiaries. An agency must allocate staff and money among more possible violations than it can pursue. The FDA examples show that priority-setting can reflect expected health benefits, public anxiety, political attention, and demands generated by emergencies. The historical inspector and budget figures illustrate this constraint and are not presented as current agency staffing.

Disclosure of enforcement criteria promotes predictability and voluntary compliance, but can weaken deterrence or expose compromises that the public finds disturbing. The FDA’s publication of food-contaminant action levels illustrates both effects. The NLRB examples distinguish broad discretion whether to prosecute from a refusal based on a mistaken legal deadline. The SEC no-action cases raise another institutional issue: attaching review only when agency leadership explains or approves a staff choice may discourage internal review and reason-giving.

The packet begins with the final page of a tribal-recognition discussion whose case caption appears outside the supplied assigned range. That passage explains that an agency’s own regulations may supply judicially manageable criteria even in a traditionally political area; merely promulgating a regulation does not suffice if its terms lack usable standards. No case identity or omitted factual history is inferred.
